_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 02:58:52Z)**_

### Annotation 1

Created a 48-unit synthetic HOA resident directory: [synthetic_residents.csv](C:\Users\OMEN\Desktop\Voice%20Agent\data\synthetic_residents.csv).

It contains only the six fields the current agent needs:

- tenant isolation: `management_company_id`, `community_id`
- resident identity: `resident_id`, `first_name`
- caller matching and maintenance context: `phone`, `unit`

This is deliberately smaller than a real property-management export. Platforms commonly also hold email, lease/occupancy dates, status, and other data, but your current flow neither uses nor should receive those fields yet. The field choice aligns with real platform patterns: property systems identify residents using unit/property plus name and phone/contact details. [AppFolio API](https://www.appfolio.com/stack/partners/api), [Buildium resident profiles](https://www.buildium.com/features/document-storage/).

All 48 records are synthetic, use fictional 555 phone numbers, and passed checks for UUIDs, E.164 phone format, and unique resident/phone/unit records. It is not wired into the current fake adapter yet.

_**User (2026-07-28 03:04:32Z)**_

What if the user calls from a different number?


---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 03:04:36Z)**_

If the phone number is not in the CSV, the agent treats them as an unknown caller.

For normal questions, it asks for their name and unit number before continuing. For emergencies—such as gas, fire, flooding, or entrapment—it does not delay: it creates the emergency workflow and transfers to on-call, even without a matched resident.

Important limitation: name + unit is only an intake fallback, not strong identity verification. Before exposing account-specific information or accepting sensitive requests, production should verify a one-time SMS code or use the caller’s authenticated resident-portal identity.

Now every caller gets a persistent, per-community database profile keyed by phone number:

_**User (2026-07-28 03:15:19Z)**_

Where does the agent stores the information?


---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 03:15:24Z)**_

It stores it in the application database, in the new `caller_profiles` table.

By default, that is the local SQLite file:

[hoa_voice_agent.db](</C:/Users/OMEN/Desktop/Voice Agent/hoa_voice_agent.db>)

The table stores:

- caller phone number
- community and management-company IDs
- caller-provided name and unit
- `identity_status` (`unverified`)
- profile creation time

Each call is also saved separately in the `conversations` table, while maintenance requests go into `work_orders`.

For PostgreSQL, set `DATABASE_URL`; the same tables are created there automatically.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 03:55:42Z)**_

Not broadly, no. Right now it is intentionally **rule-based**, not “smart” in the LLM sense.

It catches correction requests built around verbs such as:

- “change my unit number to 304”
- “update my apartment to 304”
- “correct my flat, it is 304”
- “fix my name to Ishan”

It will not reliably understand free-form variants such as:

- “No, that’s wrong—I live in 304.”
- “I moved apartments.”
- “The unit you have is incorrect.”
- “Please replace the old details.”

That restraint is deliberate: profile data should not change because the agent merely inferred a correction. The right upgrade is a hybrid:

1. LLM detects likely correction intent and extracts the proposed value.
2. Deterministic validation checks the value format.
3. Agent asks for explicit confirmation.
4. Only “yes” persists it.

That gives natural conversation handling without making profile updates unsafe.

6. Harden the voice stack.

The best immediate implementation sequence is: **remove the synthetic resident CSV → complete caller-profile enrollment → add OTP verification → build a small staff dashboard.**

_**User (2026-07-28 04:09:19Z)**_

Build community configuration.
Give each HOA a real directory of approved facts: office hours, amenities, parking rules, emergency policy, on-call contacts, and vendor routing. This is more important than making the agent more “creative.”

What do you mean by that?


---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 04:09:26Z)**_

It means creating a separate, trusted “knowledge profile” for each HOA/community.

The caller directory answers: “Who is calling?”
Community configuration answers: “What is true for this property, and who should handle this issue?”

For Pine Grove, it could contain:

| Category | Example |
|---|---|
| Office | hours, office phone, after-hours policy |
| Amenities | pool hours, gym rules, booking requirements |
| Parking | visitor rules, towing process, permit information |
| Emergency policy | what counts as emergency, immediate instructions |
| Escalation | on-call manager phone and when to transfer |
| Vendor routing | plumber for leaks, electrician for outages, elevator contractor |
| Approved FAQs | exact answers the agent is allowed to give |

Today, some of this is hard-coded in the demo adapter—pool hours, parking text, on-call phone. In a real system, it should live in database tables or an admin dashboard, scoped to each community.

Why it matters: the agent must never invent a pool time, towing rule, vendor, or emergency instruction. It should answer only from that community’s approved configuration; if a fact is missing, it should say it cannot confirm and create a follow-up or transfer the call.

---

_**User (2026-07-28 04:15:13Z)**_

What  good will that do?


---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 04:15:18Z)**_

It makes the agent useful without making it dangerous.

Without community configuration, the agent can only say generic things or guess. With it, it can reliably do real work:

- Answer “Can my guest park overnight?” using that HOA’s actual rule.
- Tell a resident the correct pool hours instead of inventing them.
- Route “water leaking in Building B” to the correct emergency/on-call process.
- Send routine HVAC issues to the right maintenance vendor.
- Know that one community treats a broken gate as urgent while another routes it to security.
- Keep different HOAs isolated—Pine Grove’s rules never leak into another property.

Business-wise, this reduces repetitive calls to staff, prevents bad guidance, gets emergencies to the right person faster, and gives managers control over what the AI is allowed to say and do.

The agent becomes a 24/7 front desk plus maintenance dispatcher—not just a chatbot that sounds helpful.

Implemented the database-backed community knowledge base.

The agent now reads approved, active facts from `community_knowledge`, scoped to the caller’s community. It no longer relies on hard-coded FAQ answers.

The initial Pine Grove knowledge includes:

- office hours and office phone
- pool and gym hours
- guest parking and towing rules
- trash schedule
- after-hours emergency policy
- water-leak and HVAC routing guidance

This is demo seed data; the natural next upgrade is an admin dashboard where HOA staff can add, edit, activate, or retire facts without touching code.

@'
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect("hoa_voice_agent.db")
for row in db.execute("""

    FROM community_knowledge
    ORDER BY category, topic

This is not a microphone or STT issue. Your screenshot proves it: the mic meter moves, but the same old session is being reused.

I verified you already have the latest installed Pipecat runtime (`1.6.0`) and latest prebuilt Playground (`1.0.5`). The immediate workaround is a browser refresh before reconnecting.

For the actual product, we should replace this development Playground with our own small call UI that creates a completely new client/session on every Connect. The Playground is explicitly meant for development and quick testing, not production call lifecycle behavior. [Pipecat prebuilt client](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat-prebuilt)

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 05:27:57Z)**_

Yes—but the fix belongs in the browser client, not the voice agent.

The Playground is a test UI. It keeps its old browser-side client after Disconnect, while our server intentionally ends the corresponding call. On the next Connect it tries to revive an object that no longer has an agent behind it.

The real fix is to replace `/client/` for this project with our own call screen whose Disconnect flow:

1. Fully disposes the current WebRTC client.
2. Clears its session and participant IDs.
3. Creates a brand-new client object on the next Connect.
4. Calls `/start` again and waits for a new agent before enabling the microphone.

That will make repeated connect/disconnect work normally, without refresh. I can build that next; it is the right production-grade solution rather than trying to patch the Playground’s state.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 05:36:02Z)**_

Yes—real incoming Twilio calls are now wired into the agent.

What happens now:

- A caller dials your Twilio number.
- Twilio calls `/twilio/voice`.
- The app validates Twilio’s signature and returns `<Connect><Stream>`.
- Twilio opens the secure audio stream to the agent.
- The agent uses the caller’s real phone number for their caller profile, so known callers retain context and unknown callers create an unverified profile.
- Both the HTTP webhook and WebSocket handshake are signature-validated.

Changed: [bot.py](C:/Users/OMEN/Desktop/Voice%20Agent/src/hoa_voice_agent/voice/bot.py), [twilio_voice.py](C:/Users/OMEN/Desktop/Voice%20Agent/src/hoa_voice_agent/voice/twilio_voice.py), and [README.md](C:/Users/OMEN/Desktop/Voice%20Agent/README.md). Verified: 48 tests pass; lint passes.

Your current process is still the old browser WebRTC server. Stop it, then:

1. Start a public tunnel:

```powershell
ngrok http 7860
```

2. Copy its `https://...` public address into `.env`:

```env
TWILIO_VOICE_WEBHOOK_URL=https://your-domain.ngrok.app/twilio/voice
TWILIO_VOICE_STREAM_URL=wss://your-domain.ngrok.app/ws
TWILIO_VALIDATE_WEBHOOKS=true
```

3. Start the phone runtime:

```powershell
python -m hoa_voice_agent.voice.bot -t twilio --host 0.0.0.0
```

4. In Twilio Console → Phone Numbers → your number → Voice Configuration, set **A call comes in** to:

```text
POST https://your-domain.ngrok.app/twilio/voice
```

Then call the Twilio number from another phone.

The stream must be publicly reachable over secure `wss://`; Twilio uses bidirectional Media Streams specifically for AI phone conversations. [Twilio Media Streams](https://www.twilio.com/docs/voice/media-streams), [Twilio webhook security](https://www.twilio.com/docs/usage/security?display=embedded)

One remaining production item: emergency transfers still use the fake call-control adapter. The call can reach the agent now, but we should implement real Twilio on-call transfer next before treating emergency escalation as live.

_**User (2026-07-28 07:43:58Z)**_

What business problem are we solving with this voice agent? Like what is the genuine pain point? Like If I have to make another person understand about our initiative what will you tell him


---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 07:44:12Z)**_

We’re solving the “front-desk overload” problem for apartment communities and HOAs.

Today, residents call management with repetitive but important issues:

- “What are the guest parking rules?”
- “What time does the pool close?”
- “My pipe is leaking—who do I contact?”
- “Can you create a maintenance request?”
- “I’m a new resident; here is my unit number.”

Staff spend a lot of time answering the same questions, manually recording details, chasing incomplete information, and deciding whether something is urgent. Calls after office hours are especially messy: residents wait, messages are missed, and genuine emergencies can be routed too slowly.

Our voice agent becomes a 24/7 community concierge and maintenance intake line. A resident calls a normal phone number; the agent recognizes their caller number when possible, collects or corrects name/unit information when needed, answers only from approved community rules, and turns maintenance requests into tracked work orders.

The important part is that it is not just “an AI chatbot on a phone.” It is an operations layer:

- It knows the community’s approved information.
- It creates a caller profile for any number, instead of assuming the caller is already in a directory.
- It keeps transcripts, corrections, work orders, failures, and escalations visible to staff.
- It follows deterministic emergency rules rather than letting an AI guess.
- It gives management a dashboard of what residents are calling about.

A simple pitch:

> We are building an AI-powered 24/7 phone front desk for residential communities. It answers resident questions using approved HOA knowledge, captures maintenance issues with the right resident context, identifies emergencies quickly, and gives property managers a clear operational record—reducing repetitive calls while improving response time and accountability.

The business value is fewer staff interruptions, better after-hours coverage, faster maintenance triage, consistent information, and fewer lost or poorly documented resident requests.

Yes—definitely. This is a real, competitive category.

| Competitor | Focus | How close they are |
|---|---|---|
| EliseAI | Large multifamily AI platform: voice, resident support, maintenance, leasing, PMS/CRM sync | Very direct, especially for enterprise apartments |
| Latchel | AI call center plus 24/7 maintenance triage and vendor dispatch | Very direct for maintenance-heavy property managers |
| Betterbot | Multifamily voice/SMS/email/chat for leasing and resident operations | Direct, broader omnichannel platform |
| Homeline | HOA-focused AI for calls, SMS, policies, tickets, and resident communication | Probably the closest HOA-specific competitor |
| RingReady / Brickwise / TenantThread | AI receptionists for property-management calls and maintenance intake | Similar workflow, typically narrower products |

EliseAI already markets voice calls, work-order triage, emergency routing, transcripts, and PMS sync; it is the strongest “big-company” benchmark. [EliseAI VoiceAI](https://eliseai.com/voiceai), [EliseAI maintenance](https://eliseai.com/maintenance) Latchel also explicitly sells an AI call center and maintenance dispatch system. [Latchel](https://latchel.com/) Homeline is notable because it is aimed at HOA management specifically. [Homeline](https://www.usehomewise.com/)

The honest view: our current product is not yet differentiated by features alone. “AI answers phone calls and creates maintenance tickets” is already being sold.

Our best positioning would be:

> An auditable, HOA-specific operations voice agent for communities that need trusted answers and safe escalation—not a generic leasing chatbot.

The potential differentiation is:

- HOA/condo-first, rather than primarily leasing-first.
- Community-controlled knowledge: the agent only answers from approved HOA rules and policies.
- Caller-created profiles: any caller can be onboarded conversationally; no perfect resident directory required.
- Deterministic emergency policy and auditable escalation, rather than an LLM deciding what is urgent.
- Clear operations dashboard: transcript, profile corrections, work orders, failures, and escalation history.
- Easier entry point for small and medium HOAs that may be too small for an enterprise platform like EliseAI.

But those are currently a product direction, not a durable moat. A real moat would come from deep integrations with property-management systems, proven emergency-routing accuracy, HOA-specific policy templates, historical operational data, and distribution through HOA management companies.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 07:59:58Z)**_

Yes — this can become profitable, but only if we sell it as an **operations product for community-management companies**, not as “an AI chatbot for an HOA.”

The real customer should be a property/HOA management company managing many communities. They already lose time and money on:

- after-hours calls and voicemail
- repetitive rule/amenity/parking questions
- incomplete maintenance requests
- emergency calls routed slowly or incorrectly
- staff manually documenting every conversation

Your agent can answer calls 24/7, identify the caller, use community-specific rules, create a structured work order, escalate emergencies deterministically, and leave an auditable transcript. That is a real operational service.

The market is real, but competitive. EliseAI and Latchel already sell AI voice/maintenance operations. Latchel, for example, combines a 24/7 maintenance engine and AI call center; EliseAI handles resident calls, transcripts, CRM/PMS syncing, escalations, and analytics. That proves customers will pay—but it also means our advantage cannot merely be “we answer phone calls.” [Latchel](https://latchel.com/), [EliseAI VoiceAI](https://eliseai.com/voiceai)

Our best positioning:

> “The auditable after-hours HOA operations desk: every caller identified, every rule answer sourced from the community’s approved knowledge, every issue captured, and every emergency routed under deterministic policy.”

That is especially suitable for HOAs, where each community has different parking, amenity, guest, emergency, and vendor rules.

A practical pricing model:

| Plan | Customer | Price idea | Includes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Pilot | 1–3 communities | $750–$2,000 setup + $299–$499/month | Knowledge-base setup, after-hours calls, maintenance intake |
| Community | One HOA | $349–$699/month | Included call minutes, transcripts, work-order creation, dashboard |
| Portfolio | Management company | $0.75–$1.50 per door/month, with a $350–$500/community floor | Multi-community configuration, routing, reporting, integrations |
| Overage | High call volume | $0.50–$0.90/minute | Protects margins on unusually busy communities |

The floor matters. HOA management software itself commonly charges per unit with a minimum; PayHOA lists $0.55 per unit/month with a $275 monthly minimum for larger communities. A voice operations layer should not be priced below the core management system when it is replacing after-hours operational work. [PayHOA pricing](https://www.payhoa.com/pricing/)

Could it be profitable? Yes, if we control call costs and avoid unlimited usage.

Illustrative unit economics:

| Example community | Monthly revenue | AI/telephony cost assumption | Gross profit |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 300–500 calls minutes/month | $499 | $150 | $349 / 70% |
| 800 call minutes/month | $699 | $260 | $439 / 63% |

These are planning assumptions, not verified production numbers. Twilio is usage-based; its US pricing includes Media Streams at $0.0044/minute, with other telephony, transcription, model, TTS, compute, recording, and support costs added on top. [Twilio Voice pricing](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/voice/pricing/us)

So the key financial rule is: **never sell unlimited AI calling at a low flat price.** Include minutes, measure usage, then charge overages. Aim for at least ~65% gross margin before sales/support costs.

What I would sell first:

1. After-hours answering and maintenance intake.
2. Community-approved FAQ: parking, pool, gates, amenities, office hours.
3. Structured work-order creation with photos/SMS links later.
4. Deterministic emergency escalation and human handoff.
5. Operations dashboard and monthly “calls avoided / issues routed / emergency response” report.

What I would not sell initially:

- legal advice or rule enforcement decisions
- payments or account-balance discussions
- autonomous vendor spending
- a promise that the AI “handles all emergencies” without live transfer and audited escalation coverage

The first commercial motion should be a paid 30-day pilot with one management company and 1–3 communities. Measure answer rate, work-order completeness, escalation speed, call containment, staff time saved, and wrong-routing rate. If those numbers are strong, expand across that company’s portfolio.

So: **yes, this can make money.** The viable business is not a cheap phone bot; it is a per-community operational platform with a setup fee, monthly platform minimum, included usage, and portfolio expansion.

It uses an English `EN-US` support voice, and the community knowledge, prompts, intent handling, profile corrections, and emergency rules are written/tested in English.

Technically, the speech layer can be expanded:

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 08:14:36Z)**_

Hindi voice mode is now wired in.

- Caller can say **“Speak Hindi”** / **“Hindi please”**, or speak in Devanagari.
- The agent switches to the Hindi NVIDIA voice for that call.
- Community answers are instructed to respond in Hindi while faithfully translating approved HOA facts.
- Hindi fire, smoke, gas, flooding, and elevator phrases now enter the deterministic emergency workflow; the safety instructions are spoken in Hindi too.
- English remains the default for every new call.

To test, restart the voice process, then call and say:

> Speak Hindi  
> पार्किंग के नियम क्या हैं?

The configuration is documented in [.env.example](C:\Users\OMEN\Desktop\Voice Agent\.env.example) and [setup.md](C:\Users\OMEN\Desktop\Voice Agent\setup.md). The Hindi voice is set to `Magpie-Multilingual.HI-IN.Sofia.Neutral`, from NVIDIA’s multilingual TTS support. [NVIDIA TTS support matrix](https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/speech/latest/reference/support-matrix/tts.html)

One remaining boundary: profile intake/corrections (name and unit) are still optimized for English phrasing. Hindi FAQ and emergency use is now supported; fully native Hindi intake is the next focused improvement.

Verified: **51 tests passed** and lint is clean.

Fixed the actual issue.

Whisper was set to `auto`, detected a GPU path, then failed because `cublas64_12.dll` is not installed. I changed it to the reliable Windows configuration:

```env
VOICE_STT_PROVIDER=local_whisper
WHISPER_DEVICE=cpu
WHISPER_COMPUTE_TYPE=int8
```

I also updated the project defaults and setup docs so new installs do not hit this CUDA failure.

The Twilio voice runtime is now restarted and confirmed running on port 7860 with:

> STT provider: local_whisper; Whisper device: cpu; compute: int8

Try calling the agent again. It should now transcribe your voice instead of failing after you speak. CPU mode may be a little slower than a correctly configured NVIDIA GPU, but it is the correct stable path on this machine.

Verified: **52 tests passed** and lint is clean.

voice    = Magpie-Multilingual.HI-IN.Sofia

Separate note: `ResourceExhausted ... request limit reached (32/32)` is an NVIDIA LLM capacity limit caused by too many rapid requests. It is unrelated to the Hindi voice selection; wait briefly and retry if it appears.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 09:20:29Z)**_

I found two likely causes in our current setup:

1. We are using NVIDIA Magpie TTS, which is not giving us reliable, natural Hindi delivery.
2. Our pipeline changes the TTS voice/language immediately before each response while LLM text is streaming. That can make audio start late, fragment oddly, or sound out of sync—especially when changing between English and Hindi. This is an architectural inference from our live pipeline; we would confirm it with TTS timing logs.

My recommendation: replace NVIDIA TTS with **ElevenLabs Flash v2.5**.

It is the strongest practical option for this agent because it supports both English and Hindi, is designed for low-latency streaming (ElevenLabs claims about 75 ms), and Pipecat has a native real-time WebSocket TTS integration with word timing and interruption handling. That is much better suited to phone conversations than our current provider path. [ElevenLabs TTS capabilities](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/overview/capabilities/text-to-speech) [Pipecat ElevenLabs service](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/server/services/tts/elevenlabs)

Options:

| Option | English | Hindi | Best use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ElevenLabs Flash v2.5 — recommended** | Natural, fast | Supported | Live HOA calls and Hinglish |
| ElevenLabs Multilingual v2 | Higher naturalness | Supported | If quality matters more than speed |
| Azure Speech | Strong Indian voices | `hi-IN` and `en-IN` voices | Enterprise / Azure-hosted deployment |

Azure is a credible alternative because it offers dedicated Indian English and Hindi neural voices, including voices that support both `en-IN` and `hi-IN`. [Azure language and voice support](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-in/azure/ai-services/speech-service/language-support)

I would not keep trying to tune Magpie. The clean next step is:

- Add an ElevenLabs API key.
- Pick one professional English/Indian-English voice and one native Hindi voice.
- Replace NVIDIA TTS fully.
- Keep Deepgram for STT and NVIDIA only for the LLM.
- Add timing metrics for speech-end → first audio, so we measure improvement rather than judge by feel alone.

That gives us a cleaner stack:

```text
Caller → Deepgram STT → HOA workflow + LLM → ElevenLabs streaming TTS → Caller
```

Get the API key from the [ElevenLabs dashboard](https://elevenlabs.io/app/settings/api-keys). Once you add `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` to `.env`, I can replace the output pipeline.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 09:30:27Z)**_

Yes—switching the conversational brain away from Nemotron is sensible.

But use **Groq** (the inference provider), not **Grok** (xAI’s model). I would **not** choose `llama-3.3-70b-versatile` now: Groq has announced it will be shut down for developer/free-tier use on **August 16, 2026**. [Groq deprecation notice](https://console.groq.com/docs/deprecations)

Use this instead:

```env
GROQ_LLM_MODEL=qwen/qwen3.6-27b
```

Qwen 3.6 27B is the better Hindi/Hinglish candidate: Groq lists it as multilingual and capable of low-latency non-thinking dialogue at about 500 tokens/sec. [Qwen 3.6 on Groq](https://console.groq.com/docs/model/qwen/qwen3.6-27b)

Alternative: `openai/gpt-oss-120b` is stronger overall and multilingual, but is heavier than we need for quick HOA calls. [GPT-OSS 120B on Groq](https://console.groq.com/docs/model/openai/gpt-oss-120b)

The architecture should be:

```text
Deepgram → deterministic emergency policy → Groq Qwen conversational LLM → TTS
```

The emergency leak response remains deterministic—an LLM must never decide whether a flood is urgent. But greetings, FAQs, clarification, and normal Hindi conversation should go through the Groq model.

Add this to `.env`:

```env
GROQ_API_KEY=your_key
GROQ_LLM_MODEL=qwen/qwen3.6-27b
```

Get the key from [Groq Console](https://console.groq.com/keys). Once added, I’ll replace the Nemotron LLM path with Groq’s native streaming Pipecat service.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-terra 2026-07-28 09:35:01Z)**_

This is not an LLM issue. The stored text contains `Ishan`, but the Hindi Magpie voice is dropping the Latin-script name.

Magpie supports Hindi, but English names inside Hindi text need an explicit pronunciation override; NVIDIA supports this through SSML phonemes or a custom pronunciation dictionary. [NVIDIA TTS customization](https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/speech/latest/tts/customization.html)

The right product fix is:

- Keep the real profile name unchanged: `Ishan`
- Store a separate speech-only pronunciation: `ईशान`
- In Hindi sessions, say the speech name; in English sessions, say `Ishan`
- Ask a new caller once: “How should I pronounce your name in Hindi?” only when needed

That prevents us from guessing or corrupting caller data. For your current profile, the Hindi spoken form should be `ईशान`, so the greeting becomes:

> वापस स्वागत है, ईशान, यूनिट 737। मैं आपकी कैसे मदद कर सकती हूँ?

I would implement this as a `spoken_name_hi` field on the caller profile—not hard-code your name into the agent.

The blandness is coming from Magpie’s generic Hindi voice—not from the LLM. Better wording cannot create vocal depth if the TTS model has flat prosody.

The fix is to upgrade the output stack:

- Use a high-quality voice provider such as **ElevenLabs**.
- Pick one warm, professional Indian-English voice and one native Hindi voice—test both with real HOA scripts, not demo sentences.
- Keep one selected voice for the whole call, as we now do.
- Use streaming audio so the response starts quickly.
- Add pronunciation rules for names, unit labels, building names, and vendor names.
- Make agent responses speech-friendly: short sentences, punctuation for pauses, no long dense paragraphs.

My recommended setup:

| Need | Model |
|---|---|
| Best natural conversational quality | Eleven Multilingual v2 |
| Lowest latency while retaining Hindi + English | Eleven Flash v2.5 |
| Avoid | Overly expressive “character” voices or generic neutral Magpie |

For this HOA agent, I’d start with **ElevenLabs Flash v2.5** and choose a calm Indian-accented voice. It supports Hindi and English, streaming, and is built for low-latency calls. [ElevenLabs model comparison](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/overview/capabilities/text-to-speech) [streaming API](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-api/guides/how-to/text-to-speech/streaming)

The other half is phonemes/pronunciation: `Ishan`, `Unit 737`, “Pine Grove,” and building names need a speech-pronunciation layer. NVIDIA supports phoneme and dictionary overrides, but switching providers will still need this for perfect names. [NVIDIA pronunciation customization](https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/speech/latest/tts/customization.html)

Once you add an `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY`, I can replace Magpie and give you a real voice-selection configuration for English and Hindi.

Yes—**Cartesia is probably the better choice for this project**.

For your specific problems—flat voice, audio not synchronized, interruptions, Hindi/Hinglish, names and unit numbers—I would choose **Cartesia Sonic 3.5 over ElevenLabs** as the first implementation.

Why it fits:

- Sonic 3.5 supports both **English and Hindi**, plus Indian languages.
- It is built for streaming conversations with natural pacing and emotional control.
- Its Pipecat WebSocket integration gives word timestamps and interruption handling, which directly helps the sync problem.
- It supports pronunciation dictionaries, so we can explicitly make `Ishan` speak as `ईशान`, without changing the stored profile name.
- Use **sentence aggregation**, not token-by-token TTS. That gives natural sentences without delayed, fragmented speech. [Cartesia Sonic 3.5](https://docs.cartesia.ai/build-with-cartesia/tts-models/latest) [Pipecat Cartesia integration](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/server/services/tts/cartesia) [custom pronunciations](https://docs.cartesia.ai/build-with-cartesia/capability-guides/custom-pronunciations)

Recommended configuration:

```text
TTS provider: Cartesia
Model: sonic-3.5
Transport: WebSocket
Aggregation: sentence
English session: English/Indian-English voice
Hindi session: Hindi voice
```

Do not use a generic multilingual voice blindly. We should select and test one Hindi voice and one professional English voice in Cartesia’s voice library against:

- “वापस स्वागत है, ईशान, यूनिट 737”
- “मेरे घर का pipe leak हो रहा है”
- emergency instructions
- unit numbers and HOA names

Get a `CARTESIA_API_KEY` from Cartesia, add it to `.env`, and I’ll replace Magpie with Cartesia Sonic 3.5.
